explain.summary: Two tanks ran low at once for Ama. Water: in 95 °F heat she sweats well over a litre an hour, and a few sips at half-time can't keep up — by the end she has lost about 4% of her body weight, and above 2% performance drops in the heat. Fuel: a soccer game uses up a lot of muscle fuel anyway, and seven hours without food left her liver's sugar store low, so the second half got harder still.
rules: Sweat rate rises with heat and with how much her position runs; water drunk at half-time replaces some.
Water lost is shown as a share of body weight; above about 2% sprinting suffers in the heat.
Muscle fuel drops during any full game; hours without food also run down the liver's sugar store, and a half-time snack tops it up.
Sprint speed = fresh speed minus game fatigue, minus the low-fuel effect, minus the dehydration effect.

source.fact: Sweating rates above 1 litre an hour are common in the heat; losing more than 2% of body weight usually hurts endurance performance in warm conditions but not in cool ones.
In a soccer game thigh-muscle fuel (glycogen) fell by about 40%, and about half the fibres were nearly empty by the end.
Sprints were about 3% slower at the end of a game and about 4% slower after hard spells in the second half.
The liver's glycogen store keeps blood sugar steady; it runs down over hours without food, and repeated sprinting drains muscle glycogen quickly.

choice.what: Sweat rate rises in a straight line with air temperature
choice.why: Real sweat rates also depend on humidity, sun and the person; the line gives about 1.6 L/h at 95 °F.

choice.what: Above 1% water loss, each extra 1% slows sprints by 1.5%
choice.why: Studies agree dehydration hurts performance in heat but not on one exact number.

choice.what: Skipping lunch acts through the liver's store, not the muscles
choice.why: After a normal breakfast her muscles start full; it's the blood-sugar supply that runs short later.

choice.what: The thirst signal switches on at about 1% water loss
choice.why: Thirst usually starts around this level, but varies between people.

illustrative: Ama's weight, her single cup of water, the 95 °F heat and the percentages are made up for a fictional story.

citations.title: Hypohydration and Human Performance: Impact of Environment and Physiological Mechanisms (Sports Medicine)
citations.supports: Sweating rates above 1 litre per hour are common in heat; losing more than 2% of body mass to dehydration usually impairs aerobic performance in warm-hot conditions but not in cool ones, and raises heart rate at a given effort.

citations.title: Muscle and Blood Metabolites during a Soccer Game: Implications for Sprint Performance (Med Sci Sports Exerc)
citations.publisher: University of the Faroe Islands research portal
citations.supports: During a soccer game thigh-muscle glycogen fell from about 449 to 255 units and about half the fibres were nearly empty; sprints were about 2.8% slower after the game and 3.6% slower after intense second-half periods.

citations.title: Glycogen
citations.supports: The liver's glycogen store is mainly used to keep blood sugar steady; after 12–24 hours of fasting liver glycogen is almost used up; muscle glycogen fuels the muscles and repeated sprinting can lower it quickly.

does: Shows water and fuel running down together over a hot game
Shows that a drink fixes one problem and food the other
Shows heat, position and body size changing the water loss
doesnt: Measure any real person — Ama is fictional
Model heat illness or anything dangerous
Tell anyone how much to drink or eat
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Feeling dizzy, sick or confused in the heat is a reason to stop, get into the shade, drink and tell a coach or adult.
